item.title: New structures come into view in brain wiring maps
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Clean-up failed for this item, so the body is a truncated excerpt of the original.)

Why it is here: Clear reporting on a significant scientific advancement with useful vocabulary and context.

New structures come into view in brain wiring maps

Sadie Harley

Scientific Editor

Robert Egan

Senior Editor

Researchers at Harvard Medical School and the University of California San Diego have sped up a powerful imaging technique enough to map, for the first time, large volumes of brain tissue in nanoscale detail. The approach reveals fine structures that brain wiring maps, known as connectomes, can miss.

The work, described in Nature Methods, promises to help scientists build more complete diagrams of how cells in the brain are connected. This, in turn, could deepen understanding of nervous-system development and certain brain diseases.

"We can now see brain structures that we haven't been able to see before in connectomics data," said co-senior author Wei-Chung Allen Lee, associate professor of neurobiology at HMS and HMS associate professor of neurology at Boston Children's Hospital.

"We hope this work will help us understand how nervous systems are built; what changes with age; and what goes awry in neurodevelopmental, cognitive, and neurodegenerative disorders," Lee said.

The gaps in brain wiring maps

Neuroscientists build connectomes to understand how neurons work together to produce thought and behavior.

Some research efforts chart the brain's major highways using MRI scans. Others zoom in, using electron microscopy to trace individual neurons and the synapses where they meet, as in a recently completed connectome of the fruit fly brain and nerve cord that Lee co-led with researchers from around the world.

However, even these fine-grained maps give up some detail when imaging large amounts of tissue. Electrical synapses, also called gap junctions, are among the key structures they can miss.

Fewer images, thicker tissue samples

To capture that detail, the team turned to electron tomography, a technique that builds 3D images by viewing a sample from multiple angles. Electron tomography is usually slow because it requires taking hundreds of images of the same area.

The researchers found that they could use about 50 times fewer images than standard electron tomography, on tissue sections roughly 20 times thicker than usual, and still achieve 3D resolution of about 15 nanometers or finer.

Hidden connections and cellular exchanges

Applying the technique to tissue from the mouse cerebellum, the team saw electrical synapses, which let signals pass almost instantly between neurons and are thought to help synchronize network activity.

They also saw tiny protrusions extending between neurons and neighboring support cells called glia. The researchers say these structures appear to be involved in one cell taking up material from another.

"We're seeing uncharacterized structures, suggesting that neurons are 'nibbling' their neighboring cells," Lee said.

In addition, the team traced nerve fibers through a 3D block of tissue to the points where those fibers connect with other neurons.

Scaling the approach to an entire mammalian brain will take more work, including automating how tissue samples are handled, the researchers said. That is a long-term goal for the team.

Publication details

Aaron T. Kuan et al., Scalable electron tomography for connectomics, Nature Methods (2026). DOI: 10.1038/s41592-026-03345-x

Journal information: Nature Methods

item.title: Stress and anxiety are wearing workers down: How to spot your triggers and cope
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: Important topic with clear reporting and useful information for understanding workplace mental health.

Stress and anxiety are wearing workers down: How to spot your triggers and cope

Workplace stress and anxiety. Who hasn't experienced it?

However, if that anxiety is so strong that it hurts your performance or lingers for months, you might have a problem, one expert says.

For many workers, the strain isn't easing up. About 1 in 3 employees in a recent global survey said they're "merely surviving," and 1 in 4 said their mental health had gotten worse over the past year.

Half said they had a hard time staying focused or engaged at work.

Those numbers come from the 2026 State of Workforce Mental Health report by Lyra Health, a company that provides mental health benefits to employers. It surveyed 7,500 workers in six countries, including the United States, in late 2025.

Dr. Asim Shah, executive vice chair of psychiatry and behavioral sciences at Baylor College of Medicine in Houston, explains what can trigger workplace anxiety, how to manage it and when to seek professional help.

"The goal is not to suffer and not let your anxiety affect work performance," he said. "About 60% of people experience workplace anxiety. It is common, which means you can do something about it."

Surly co-workers, a demanding supervisor, small, annoying tasks or overwhelming major projects can cause workplace anxiety.

Bigger worries play a part, too. Money problems were the most common source of ongoing stress in the Lyra survey (57%). Heavier workloads (35%) and fear of losing a job (23%) came next.

Artificial intelligence is adding another layer. Nearly half of the workers surveyed said AI at work made them feel they always had to be available (46%), and a similar share said it made them anxious about job security (44%).

If you have workplace stress or anxiety, you might notice signs like:

- Feeling overly anxious or nervous

- Experiencing excessive sweating or trembling

- Obsessing about a task

- Having a lack of interest in your work

"The anxiety becomes so overwhelming that you are unable to focus and concentrate," Shah noted in a Baylor news release. "These feelings can impair your daily work functions." If that continues for more than six months, Shah said it might be time to seek professional help.

"Some employers might offer an employee assistance program where you can go for help," he said. "You can also start talking to a therapist through psychotherapy or look into medication management for your workplace anxiety."

Getting that help isn't always easy, though. Among survey respondents dealing with more complex mental health needs, 40% said they had trouble getting care through their employee assistance program (EAP), and more than half ran into long waitlists.

Leaving for a new job won't necessarily solve the problem either, Shah added, offering several suggestions to manage it and help reduce stress.

- Break your tasks into small pieces.

- Set small goals throughout the week and congratulate yourself for reaching them.

- Express your emotions. Journal how you feel. Talk, laugh or cry with someone you confide in.

- Start healthy habits and do things you enjoy.

- Work within your limits. Set boundaries with your workload.

item.title: Alcohol may weaken cancer immunotherapy, early research suggests
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: Useful information on the interaction between alcohol and cancer immunotherapy with clear detail.

Alcohol may weaken cancer immunotherapy, early research suggests

Cancer immunotherapy has transformed treatment for several advanced cancers, yet the difference between these treatments working and not could depend on simple routine habits. A recent study published in Science Signaling explores one such overlooked factor: regular alcohol consumption.

The focus was on immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs), a class of drugs that includes anti-programmed cell death protein 1 (PD-1) therapies that train the body's immune system to attack tumor cells. The researchers used a mouse model and human clinical data to investigate how regular alcohol consumption impacts the success of ICIs.

The effects were evident in both animal models and human patients. In mice with lung and bladder cancer, moderate-to-heavy alcohol consumption cut the success of immunotherapy by nearly half and increased the likelihood of tumors returning. A similar pattern emerged in human clinical data, where lung cancer patients who regularly consumed alcohol, more than one drink a week, experienced fewer survival benefits after starting anti-PD-1 treatment.

Alcohol breaks the brakes

The body's immune system relies on specialized white blood cells called T cells to seek out and destroy cancer cells. To prevent these immune cells from becoming overactive and attacking healthy tissues, T cells have natural off-switches, including a receptor protein called programmed cell death protein 1 (PD-1).

Cancer cells can hijack this mechanism by activating the PD-1 off-switch on T cells, effectively putting the brakes on the immune system and allowing tumors to escape attack. Anti-PD-1 drugs, such as pembrolizumab and nivolumab, use engineered antibodies that bind to the PD-1 receptor and block it. This releases the brakes on T cells, allowing them to recognize and attack cancer cells. While these medications have been found to be quite effective in clinical practice, some patients do not benefit from them as much as expected.

Alcohol could be one reason why. Previous studies have found that it interferes with the immune system's response against the tumor. Doctors thus actively advise cancer patients to avoid alcohol. Yet, alcohol consumption remains common among people with cancer, with one study finding that 76.4% continued to drink.

To understand how alcohol interferes with immunotherapy, the researchers turned to mice with lung and bladder cancer. For five weeks before introducing cancer cells, they gave the animals moderate or heavy amounts of alcohol to mimic human drinking habits. They then treated the mice with immunotherapy and tracked tumor growth, survival and recurrence. The researchers also examined electronic health records of cancer patients who had received anti-PD-1 treatment at the UNC Chapel Hill Cancer Hospital between 2014 and 2018.

Weakening the effect of ICI therapies

The study discovered that regular alcohol consumption significantly weakens cancer immunotherapy, but there is a way to restore its effectiveness. Moderate-to-heavy alcohol consumption reduced the success of ICI therapies by about 50% in mice, and in human patients, too, drinking more than one drink per week was associated with reduced survival benefits.

They found that alcohol exposure reduced the overall number of tumor-killing T cells (CD4+ and CD8+ T cells) entering the tumor microenvironment. It also impaired CD8+ T cell activation, reducing their ability to produce key tumor-fighting signals like interferon-gamma (IFN-γ) and kill cancer cells. Alcohol also causes T cells to express higher levels of a second inhibitory receptor called TIGIT, whose original job is to prevent immune cells from becoming overactive and attacking healthy tissues.

Antidote to alcohol's effect

To counter this effect, researchers combined standard anti-PD-1 therapy with an anti-TIGIT antibody. Blocking both PD-1 and TIGIT simultaneously prevented these two mechanisms from holding back the immune response. In alcohol-exposed mice, the combination restored complete tumor response rates to almost the same level as in mice that had not consumed alcohol.

The findings together identified the mechanism by which regular alcohol use can impair the efficacy of immune checkpoint inhibitors, like anti-PD-1 therapy against cancer. Future studies will need to use precise alcohol intake numbers to better understand how drinking affects ICIs. For that to happen, the researchers suggest that adding patients' alcohol use to cancer databases would not only help show how it affects different treatments across cancers but also help identify potential solutions.

TIGIT Gene

item.title: Independent review ordered into surgery carried out by NHS Grampian
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: Significant issue in healthcare with clear reporting and context.

Independent review ordered into surgery carried out by NHS Grampian

The Scottish government has ordered a review into hepatobiliary surgery at NHS Grampian after a whistleblower leaked a document showing 19 avoidable deaths at the health board.

Dr Mohammed Habib claimed he had contacted the Scottish government on four separate occasions and had gone to the police and the lord advocate with his concerns about patient safety at the board.

In a report from 2022, which was only released by Habib on Thursday, it was found 19 of the 31 deaths in liver and pancreatic surgery cases were avoidable.

NHS Grampian chief executive, Laura Skaife-Knight, said the board would be "open and transparent" in co-operating with the review.

Habib also said two people had died after having the wrong procedure performed on them and has called for the health board to face a corporate homicide inquiry.

Health Secretary Angela Constance said the review would assess how concerns raised about liver, gallbladder and bile duct surgery, including those by Habib, were handled by the board and the Scottish government.

She said it would identify weaknesses in governance, missed opportunities, unreasonable delay, and gaps in accountability.

Constance said Habib's concerns were "deeply concerning and of the utmost seriousness".

"Following discussion with the first minister, I am today commissioning an urgent and fully independent review of how concerns about hepatobiliary (HPB) surgery in NHS Grampian was handled, including the 2022 report into the deaths of patients who underwent HPB surgery," she said.

"Patient safety and high-quality care must always be the first concern of all those who work in, and with, the NHS."

She said that if any patients had questions or needed advice and support they should contact the NHS Grampian helpline on 08085 202030.

One patient told BBC Scotland News he "technically died" after undergoing liver surgery at Aberdeen Royal Infirmary.

Derek Appleton said he believed mistakes had been made during a procedure to remove 60% of his liver after being diagnosed with stage four cancer.

He said he lost 11 litres of blood and went into cardiac arrest, but was never given a proper explanation for what happened.

Constance will make a statement in Holyrood on Tuesday, where she is expected to lay out the timetable and announce who will lead the review.

She said: "My thoughts are with anyone who has lost a loved one and I am acutely aware of the courage it has taken Dr Habib to come forward.

"I recognise he has sought to do this repeatedly, over a number of years, to both to the Scottish government and several other bodies.

"Patients and staff in Grampian have the right to expect full transparency and independent assurance that when valid concerns are raised, they are properly and robustly pursued. That is what this review will seek to establish."

Skaife-Knight said the review was the "best way forward".

She added: "We know the allegations which have been the subject of significant media interest in recent days will cause further concern for patients and families, our communities and staff.

"We will take immediate steps to secure and preserve relevant information, files and records as part of this process."

'Dramatic action'

Humza Yousaf was health secretary at the time of Dr Habib's report.

He told BBC Scotland News he supported "further dramatic action" being taken in relation to NHS Grampian.

A spokesperson for Yousaf - who went on to become first minister before resigning in May 2024 â said: "Humza supports full transparency about what happened at NHS Grampian and will co-operate fully with any review that takes place.

"He has made it clear that he supports minutes from the period in question being released.

"As health secretary, Humza met whistleblowing champions in health boards across Scotland, and he remains clear that staff who raise patient safety concerns must be listened to and protected.

"It takes real courage to do what Dr Habib has done, and he should be commended for refusing to let these concerns go."

The Scottish government has said action will be taken quickly when required as part of the process to refer any issues â including potential criminality â to the relevant authorities without waiting for the final report.

The announcement comes after First Minister John Swinney announced a review of how the government handles correspondence, after he claimed he first heard of three letters sent to him by Habib on Thursday.

On Tuesday, Constance appointed an expert health team to oversee NHS Grampian improvements.

She said the "external intervention support team", comprising experienced senior NHS leaders, would work alongside Grampian's health team to provide "intensive turnaround support".

Healthcare Improvement Scotland has also been asked to complete an early review of NHS Grampian within three months to assess progress, followed by ongoing reviews, to provide independent assurance.

'Excruciating' wait for answers

Scottish Labour's health spokeswoman, Jackie Baillie, said the review was "welcome", adding that a similar situation "must never happen ever again".

She said: "Were it not for the bravery of Dr Habib in this week speaking out, we may never have known just how far this went.

"Grieving families who lost loved ones in the care of NHS Grampian deserve the full truth of what happened at the health board, including who knew what was going on, when they knew, and why it has taken this long for these concerns to come to light."

Yi-pei Chou Turvey, Scottish Liberal Democrat MSP for north east Scotland, said the wait for answers for the families of affected patients had been "excruciating".

She added: "SNP ministers ought to have been battering down the door of NHS Grampian after receiving multiple warnings from Dr Habib and a report uncovering 19 avoidable deaths.…

item.title: 'It gives me the ick': Can you cheat on someone with a video game?
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: Interesting topic but less relevant to the reader's interests and more focused on entertainment.

'It gives me the ick': Can you cheat on someone with a video game?

Imagine your partner spending hours flirting with someone else, trying to hold their hand and taking them on dates. Most people would have questions.

But what if that someone only exists inside a video game?

The latest instalment in Rockstar's blockbuster Grand Theft Auto franchise has already set sales records, making $3.8bn (Â£2.9bn) in its first day alone.

At the heart of the game is the relationship between its two main characters, Jason and Lucia.

Rockstar says the Bonnie and Clyde-style duo do not have to maintain a full romantic relationship to progress the game.

But their connection can grow by spending time together outside of the main crime and life-on-the-run storyline â through shopping, visiting bars and restaurants and working out together.

Smaller interactions like holding hands and quickly responding to each other's texts can help build a bond.

The idea has restarted a debate almost as old as gaming itself: if you are that invested in a fictional relationship, is your real-life partner entitled to be upset?

In September, polling company YouGov put that question to more than 4,000 British adults.

About 6% said they would regard it as cheating, while a further 19% said they would "not be okay with it". Women were considerably more likely than men to take a dim view.

Alli Franco, a 30-year-old Texan who posts anime and gaming content to more than a million followers, external on TikTok, says she felt "dismayed" watching the debate unfold online.

"If your partner is insecure about a fictional character, then there needs to be some serious reflection," she told the BBC.

"It's similar to having a crush on a TV star, but even further removed from cheating since there is no other actual person involved.â

After Franco posted a video on the subject, hundreds of commenters appeared to agree with her, although some did have reservations.

"To be honest, it depends," wrote one. "If you're cancelling plans with your significant other or directing your intimacy towards a fictional character, then that is a little odd."

"It's very odd and it really gives me the ick," another woman told us.

Mimicking social relationships

For decades, video games have allowed players to build relationships with non-player characters, or NPCs.

Gamers could marry villagers in Harvest Moon in 1996, shape emotional storylines in Final Fantasy VII and pursue more complex romances in role-playing games like Baldur's Gate II.

In life simulator The Sims, they could flirt, date, marry and have children with computer-controlled characters.

But all those interactions were tightly scripted, based on rules and storylines written in advance by game developers.

GTA 6 offers something more dynamic, allowing players to shape the relationship between Jason and Lucia through a wider range of open-world interactions and choices.

"The more sophisticated games get, the less likely it is that players get pulled out of the experience," says Arienne Ferchaud, an associate professor at Florida State University who studies how people form connections with fictional characters.

"Games are doing a better job of mimicking reality and mimicking social relationships."

Grand Theft Auto 6 may represent the current cutting edge of game design, but the next leap forward could come from artificial intelligence.

Nvidia, Ubisoft and other huge tech companies are already experimenting with generative AI systems that allow players to hold more natural conversations with NPCs.

Future characters could remember past encounters, react to a player's actions and build relationships that change over time rather than following a pre-written script.

Ferchaud believes that could make games feel even more immersive.

"You could have relationships that feel more solid or more special," she says, although she argues AI as it exists today would still be creating "a stronger illusion" rather than a genuinely meaningful connection.

Whether that is exciting or unsettling may depend on the player, and there has been some resistance to the wider use of the technology in gaming.

Franco says she is already seeing adverts for AI chatbots that let fans talk to their favourite anime characters.

"I can definitely see AI integrating into games and making it a more realistic experience," she says.

"But should that happen I would still see it as just a game. At the end of the day you can't cheat with lines of code."

Source: BBC Health | Published: 2026-11-21 21:21 UTC | Difficulty: 41/100

item.title: Cigarettes on silver platters at Bondi ‘clean’ beauty business lip gloss launch referred for investigation
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: Promotional content with potential health risks, not suitable for the reader's interests.

An Australian beauty company that promotes “clean” ingredients “free from skin irritants” has been referred to state health regulators after appearing to offer cigarettes to guests at a beachside lip gloss launch.

“Celebrating the launch of our soft gloss with our community,” one post from the event shared by the Copini Beauty account on Instagram read, with an accompanying carousel of images showing what appeared to be cigarettes on display with Copini-branded match boxes, lipglosses and glasses of wine.

The images are also featured in a highlight reel from the event on the official Instagram page for the brand.

Copini is co-founded by influencer Casey James and product developer Carla McGraw.

Under the Public Health (Tobacco and Other Products) Act 2023, advertising or promoting smoking or the use of tobacco products is prohibited. Both state and federal laws prohibit businesses offering, giving or distributing a free tobacco product.

Any tobacco supplied must also meet strict product standards, such as displaying mandatory graphic health warnings. The cigarettes at the Copini launch do not appear to carry any health warnings on the filter as required, indicating they are illicit products. Buying or supplying illicit tobacco is illegal in Australia, regardless of the quantity.

Cigarettes in Australia cannot legally carry brand logos. The cigarettes appear to carry the Manchester “sapphire blue” branding, one of the most common illicit tobacco products in Australia. They are considered unlabelled under Australian law because they do not carry official government health warnings and compliant packaging.

A spokesperson for the NSW health minister, Ryan Park, said of the event and images: “This has been referred to NSW health’s centre for regulation and enforcement.”

The centre works with state and federal authorities to regulate smoking products and has powers to inspect premises, seize illicit stock, issue fines and prosecute offenders.

A spokesperson for the federal health department said the government is “deeply concerned about advertising or promotion that glamorises smoking or the use of tobacco products, or helps normalise tobacco use, particularly where it might reach young people”.

“There is no appropriate place for tobacco products to be used as a promotional prop or to make smoking appear fashionable or appealing,” the spokesperson said.

“The government strengthened Australia’s tobacco laws to reduce the visibility and normalisation of tobacco products and protect Australians from the harms of smoking.”

The spokesperson said allegations of non-compliance with laws are taken seriously, saying the maximum penalty for criminal advertising or sponsorship of tobacco under federal laws is $728,000 for an individual, or $7.2m for a company.

Smoking accelerates ageing and causes more than 16,000 cases of cancer in Australia each year. The display of cigarettes at the launch appears to contradict Copini’s philosophy: “We’re 100% vegan, cruelty-free, and free from skin irritants and endocrine disruptors,” the website says, stating that “clean ingredients” are used in all products.

The company did not respond to requests for comment.

It comes amid growing concerns about the use of cigarettes by brands and in images of celebrities, especially online, with health experts warning it risks normalising and glamorising smoking.

Becky Freeman, a professor of tobacco control with the University of Sydney, said it was “shocking to see the resurgence” of smoking in pop culture and on red carpets.

“But to see this really local example, in Bondi, shows this is not an international phenomena – it’s happening in a country like Australia where we have low smoking rates through strong regulations and health policies,” she said.

item.title: Black Friday deals for liquid Brazilian butt lifts criticised over safety fears
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: Promotional content with safety concerns, not suitable for the reader's interests.

Clinics in England are promoting seasonal deals – including for Black Friday – on liquid Brazilian butt lifts (BBLs), despite concerns about the risks of the procedure.

The government is consulting on limiting liquid BBLs, vampire facials and deep chemical peels in England to qualified healthcare professionals. The proposals follow the death of Alice Webb, a 33-year-old mother of five, after a botched liquid BBL in a Gloucester salon in 2024. Her family have called for laws against “cosmetic cowboys” to be introduced before more people die.

A liquid BBL involves injecting dermal filler into the buttocks. Plastic surgeons say it can carry significant risks and requires expert skill and training to perform, with large amounts of filler potentially causing serious side effects such as blood clots, fat embolisms and sepsis.

The Advertising Standards Authority (ASA) has already acted against time-limited promotions, concluding that Black Friday offers could rush consumers into deciding on cosmetic surgery without enough time to consider the consequences.

Between April and December 2025, the watchdog found more than 900 ads for liquid BBLs in its advert monitoring system. During that period, only 11.5% of the ads they checked stuck to the ASA’s rules.

It said some ads made claims such as “0% infection rate” or described procedures as “safe”, without properly reflecting the risks involved. Other ads played on body insecurities, promising to “boost your confidence” or “transform your body effortlessly”.

Ashton Collins, the director of Save Face, a government-approved register of accredited non-surgical treatment practitioners, said she was “outraged” by BBLs being advertised as “party-season bargains” with time-limited discounts.

“These are not routine beauty treatments; they are serious medical procedures that can lead to devastating complications,” she said.

“Marketing them this way trivialises the risks, and pressures people to make snap decisions without the time, information or proper consultation they need to make an informed choice.”

She added that Save Face had received 1,004 patient-reported complaints about non-surgical BBLs, hip-dip and breast-augmentation procedures since 2023. More than 50% of the complainants experienced sepsis, 94% required hospital treatment and 43% required surgery.

“The impact on people’s lives can be profound and lasting,” Collins said.

One London provider, Clinic Blvd, recently advertised on social media for a 48-hour deal of 800ml of filler plus 200ml free for £1,300. The post, accompanied by a picture of a woman’s bottom, stated that demand was at “an all time high” and that the deals would not be available to everyone. The clinic also listed breast filler as an option, at £799 for 400ml.

A spokesperson for Clinic Blvd said patient safety and informed consent were its top priorities. “All treatments are subject to individual consultations and clinical suitability assessments,” they said. “We take responsible advertising seriously and remain committed to maintaining appropriate professional standards.”

An Instagram post from De Vere Signature Aesthetics, also based in London, promised 100ml of free filler as a “special limited time offer” added to procedures. Their price for filler falls as the volume rises, from about £5 per ml at the bottom of the scale to about £1.50 at the top, rewarding customers for choosing larger amounts. De Vere Signature Aesthetics was approached for comment.

The Belle Clinic, also in London, advertised a deal online offering 40% off a liquid BBL in autumn to “get ready now for your Christmas party”.

A spokesperson said: “Our current promotion is an autumn and winter seasonal offer … It is not intended to create urgency or pressure anyone into making a decision about an aesthetic procedure. We take the ASA’s guidance seriously and are willing to review our promotional wording to ensure it communicates our approach responsibly.”

Nora Nugent, a consultant plastic surgeon and former president of the British Association of Aesthetic Plastic Surgeons (BAAPS), expressed concern over time-limited discounts. “This is a sales ploy that makes people make quick decisions in case they lose out on the offer,” she said, warning that any special offers, even if not time limited, could encourage people to have treatments they might not otherwise choose.

Gerard Lambe, a consultant plastic and cosmetic surgeon and a spokesperson for BAAPS, said: “People encouraging you to have increased volumes and reduced prices, that’s the worst thing that you could ever do. [You] should never ever do that to people. It increases your risk of complications.”

However, Lambe acknowledged that some private plastic surgeons do offer deals on procedures, saying that the issue of finance is complex, and that lack of affordability could lead people to choose cheaper surgery abroad with a greater risk of complications.

The ASA said its rules made clear that adverts for liquid BBLs must be socially responsible.

“We’ve taken widespread and targeted enforcement action against advertisers breaking the rules, including by trivialising the risks of these procedures, using time-limited promotions to create a sense of urgency and exploiting women’s insecurities,” a spokesperson said.

“We support the introduction of further government measures to regulate the sector.”
